**Before the visit**
- Add the appointment date in the Visits tab. MenoMap tells you how ready your notes are and what would make them more complete.
- Choose the most important topics and questions. Keep only three or four.
- Create a note for the last 30 or 90 days. Check whether your medication list is up to date.

**During the visit**
- Hand or show the doctor the first page. It is designed to be read in under a minute: counts, averages, a heat calendar and your questions.
- Start with the question that matters most to you.
- If your doctor speaks another language, you can create the note in that language.

**What the note is, and what it is not**

It is a summary of what you entered, plus any data you choose to include from the Health app. The note is not a diagnosis or a full medical record, and any pattern in it is only a coincidence check, not evidence of cause. The doctor may ask things the note cannot answer, and that is normal.

**After the visit**

Add any new medication on the day you start it. After a few weeks, MenoMap can show your entries before and after, making the next follow-up easier.
backTranslations.42:
**Menopause** is a single point in time: the day marking 12 consecutive months without a period, when this is not due to another cause (such as pregnancy, certain medications or surgery). In many countries menopause happens on average in the early 50s, but any time from the mid-40s to mid-50s is common.

**Perimenopause** is the multi-year stage leading up to that point. Hormone levels rise and fall erratically, so periods may become irregular, heavier, lighter, closer together or further apart. Many changes people associate with menopause, such as hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and mood changes, often begin in this stage, while periods still occur. Perimenopause can last a few years or considerably longer, and each person experiences it differently.

**Postmenopause** is the whole period after that 12-month mark. Some symptoms ease over time; others may last for many years.

Menopause can also come earlier due to surgical removal of the ovaries, certain cancer treatments or other health problems. Menopause before age 40 is sometimes called premature ovarian insufficiency, and this should be discussed with a doctor.

**How it is recognised.** For many people over 45, a doctor identifies perimenopause or menopause from your history and symptoms. Blood tests are not always needed, because hormone levels fluctuate from day to day. Tests are more often used when the person is young or the situation is unclear.

**What MenoMap does and does not do.** MenoMap cannot tell you which stage you are in. What it can do is faithfully record what you notice: hot flashes, sleep, mood and treatment, so that you and your doctor look at the same picture.

backTranslations.162:
Doctors call hot flashes and night sweats **vasomotor symptoms**. A hot flash is a sudden wave of heat, usually in the face, neck and chest, sometimes with flushing, sweating, a racing heart or chills afterwards. Night sweats are the same thing happening during sleep, and can be strong enough to wake you or soak the bedsheets.

This is one of the most common changes around menopause. Some people have only a few mild episodes; others have many a day, disrupting work and sleep. For some they fade over a few years; for others they last much longer.

**What may make them more likely.** People often notice a pattern linked to alcohol, caffeine, spicy food, hot rooms, stress or heavy blankets. These vary a great deal from person to person, so tracking your own tags may be more useful than a general list.

**There are other causes too.** Flushing and sweating can also be due to thyroid disease, infection, certain medications, anxiety and other conditions. If your symptoms do not fit the usual pattern, or come with weight loss, fever or feeling unwell, tell your doctor.

**Describe it clearly.** Details useful for the visit:
- About how many episodes per day and per night
- How strong they feel and how long they last
- What they disrupt: sleep, work, conversation, exercise
- What seems to happen just before
- What you have tried, and whether anything changed

MenoMap's Hot Flash button and the after-the-fact recording are made to capture exactly these without much effort.

**Help is always available.** There are hormonal and non-hormonal treatment options, plus practical measures. Which suits you is something to discuss with your doctor.

backTranslations.291:
Hormone therapy (often called HRT or MHT) replaces part of the estrogen the body makes less of around menopause. Major guidelines describe it as an effective treatment for hot flashes and night sweats in many people, and it can also help with other symptoms.

**There are different forms:** patches, gels, sprays, tablets and low-dose vaginal products for local symptoms such as vaginal dryness. People who still have a uterus are usually prescribed a progestogen along with the estrogen to protect the uterine lining.

**Benefits and risks depend on the individual:** age, time since periods stopped, personal and family history (for example of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke or heart disease), and the type of medication and route. That is why this is a decision to make with a doctor who understands your history, not something an app can decide.

**Questions people commonly ask:**
- Is hormone therapy an option for me, and why or why not?
- Which type and form do you suggest, and why?
- What benefits can I expect, and after how long?
- What are my own risks, and how do they compare with not treating?
- What should I watch for, and when should we reassess?

**If you are taking it,** record it in MenoMap (You → Medications). MenoMap will show your hot flashes before and after you started, as a coincidence check and not evidence, so you have something concrete to discuss at follow-up.

MenoMap never suggests starting, stopping or changing a medication.

backTranslations.293:
Hormone therapy is not right for everyone, and some people simply want a different approach. There are many options.

**Prescription medication.** Some non-hormonal medications have evidence for reducing hot flashes. These include some medications originally developed for other conditions, and a newer class designed specifically for hot flashes. Each has its own benefits, side effects and interactions, so a doctor can help you weigh them.

**Talking therapy and mind-body approaches.** Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) adapted for menopause has evidence for making hot flashes and night sweats less bothersome, and for improving sleep. Clinical hypnosis has also been studied.

**Practical changes many people find helpful:**
- Dress in layers so you can quickly take some off
- A fan at your desk and by the bed
- A cooler bedroom and breathable bedding
- Recognising and reducing your own triggers (MenoMap's tags and experiments help here)
- Regular activity and a steady bedtime

**Supplements and herbal products.** Evidence for many is inconsistent or limited, quality is uneven, and some interact with other medications. Tell your doctor or pharmacist everything you are taking, including over-the-counter products.

**Try only one change at a time.** MenoMap's two-week experiment compares your own records before and during the change, which is easier to evaluate than a feeling.

backTranslations.416:
Most visits are short, and it is hard to recall on the spot the nights of a whole month. People tend to remember the most recent days or the worst days. A simple record fills that gap.

**What a diary gives the doctor:**
- How often symptoms occur and how strong they are, not just whether they occur
- Whether things are getting better, worse or staying the same
- What is going on around them: sleep, alcohol, stress, medication
- A starting point for comparison if you try a treatment

**Keep it light.** A diary is only useful if you keep it up. MenoMap is built around a one-tap Hot Flash button and a four-question evening diary, so it takes a few seconds, no whole notebook needed.

**Two weeks is a good start.** Recording for two to four weeks usually gives a clearer picture than a single bad week.

**Bring your questions too.** Write down what matters most to you: the symptom that bothers you most, what you want to try or avoid, and anything that worries you. MenoMap's Visits tab helps you choose questions and print them with your note.

backTranslations.479:
Once you have gone 12 months without a period, **any vaginal bleeding needs to be checked by a doctor**, even if it happens only once, and even if it is only spotting or a light pink or brown discharge.

Most of the time the cause turns out not to be serious. For example, thinning of the vaginal or uterine lining is common. But bleeding after menopause can sometimes be an early sign of a condition that is much easier to treat if found early. That is why public health guidance recommends getting checked rather than waiting.

**If you are on hormone therapy,** some kinds of bleeding may be expected, depending on the type you use. Bleeding that is unexpected with your treatment, heavier than usual, or happens at the wrong time also needs to be checked.

**What to do:**
- Contact your doctor or healthcare provider and say you have bleeding after menopause.
- Record the date, the amount of blood, and anything else you notice. MenoMap can save it for you (You → Cycle).

MenoMap cannot tell you why the bleeding happened. The app will remind you to get checked and include this information in your visit note.

backTranslations.529:
Poor sleep is one of the most common complaints in midlife, and it rarely has only one cause.

**Night sweats** can directly wake you, or leave you too hot or damp to fall back asleep.

**Other common contributing factors:**
- Having to get up to urinate at night
- Anxiety or a racing mind
- Alcohol, which may help you fall asleep but often breaks up the second half of the night's sleep
- Caffeine late in the day
- Pain, restless legs syndrome, or the snoring of the person next to you
- Snoring or pauses in breathing, which may be a sign of sleep apnea (worth telling a doctor, especially if you are very sleepy in the daytime)

**What often helps.** A cool, dark room; breathable bedding and easy-to-remove layers; a steady wake-up time; and less alcohol near bedtime. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is a structured, well-studied approach, and many doctors can refer you.

**What to track.** For a week or two, record your sleep score, night hot flashes, alcohol and late caffeine. MenoMap's evening diary and hot flash log do this in just a few taps. If you use an Apple Watch, MenoMap can show sleep and wrist temperature from the Health app alongside night sweats, as background information and not an explanation.

**When to get checked.** Talk to a doctor if poor sleep affects your safety (for example when driving), your mood or daily life, or if you notice moments of stopped breathing or gasping at night.
